faq.a: No; low muscle mass can mask reduced GFR, so check urine albumin or repeat creatinine over time.
faq.q: Can a normal creatinine rule out CKD in a thin patient?

faq.a: It requires less infrastructure, can be done at bedside, and uses locally available fluids.
faq.q: Why is peritoneal dialysis preferred in many African hospitals?

faq.a: When serum potassium >5.5 mmol/L, bilateral renal artery stenosis, or severe AKI (stage 3).
faq.q: When should ACE‑inhibitors be avoided in renal disease?

exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer with malaria presents with oliguria and rising creatinine – what is the next immediate step? — Assess volume status, give cautious isotonic fluids, and stop any nephrotoxic drugs.

How does you differentiate pre‑renal AKI from intrinsic ATN using simple labs? — Use BUN/creatinine ratio >20 and fractional excretion of sodium <1 % for pre‑renal; ratio <15 and FENa >2 % suggest ATN.
A patient with HIV on tenofovir develops CKD stage 3 – which antiretroviral should be switched and why? — Replace tenofovir with abacavir or zidovudine to avoid further tubular toxicity.
What are the key ultrasound findings that point to chronic kidney disease? — Small, echogenic kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation.
Why is hyperkalaemia more dangerous in CKD than in healthy kidneys? — Impaired excretion leads to rapid rise; cardiac membrane effects cause arrhythmias.

Explain why ACE‑inhibitors are both protective and potentially harmful in CKD. — They reduce intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria (protective) but can raise potassium and worsen GFR in advanced disease (harmful).

A pregnant woman in her third trimester develops flank pain and anuria – what condition must be ruled out and how? — Obstructive hydronephrosis; perform bedside ultrasound to look for dilated pelvicalyceal system.

What preventive measures reduce progression of CKD in low‑resource settings? — Blood pressure control, avoidance of NSAIDs/herbal nephrotoxins, treatment of infections, vaccination, and regular monitoring of eGFR/ACR.
ai.title: Approach to Renal Disease
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A step‑by‑step clinical framework for evaluating acute and chronic kidney disease in low‑resource settings, focusing on history, exam, staging, common tropical causes, and pragmatic investigations.

b: AKI: rise in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h or ≥1.5‑fold from baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
sections.p: Renal disease includes acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Diagnosis relies on serum creatinine, urine output, and duration of dysfunction.

t.b: Is kidney filtration reduced? – Elevated creatinine indicates reduced GFR; compare to baseline if available.
Is there oliguria or anuria? – Low output supports AKI; monitor for fluid overload.
Is there protein, blood, or leukocytes? – Protein suggests glomerular disease; blood may indicate infection or stones; leukocytes point to pyuria.

b: AKI Stage 1: 1.5‑1.9× baseline creatinine or 0.3‑0.5 mg/dL rise.
AKI Stage 2: 2.0‑2.9× baseline.
AKI Stage 3: ≥3.0× baseline, creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dL, or need for dialysis.
CKD Stage 1‑5 based on eGFR (≥90 to <15 mL/min/1.73 m²).
sections.p: Use KDIGO criteria for AKI and CKD staging for chronic disease. Staging guides urgency and need for renal replacement.

t.a: eGFR calculation (CKD‑EPI or MDRD if creatinine only)
t.b: What is the chronic functional level? – Determines CKD stage and referral timing.

b: Pre‑renal: volume depletion (diarrhoea, vomiting, malaria), sepsis, heart failure, nephrotoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs).
Intrinsic: acute tubular necrosis (sepsis, severe malaria), glomerulonephritis (post‑streptococcal, lupus), HIV‑associated nephropathy, sickle‑cell nephropathy, schistosomal interstitial disease.
Post‑renal: obstructive uropathy from stones, prostatic hypertrophy, pregnancy‑related hydronephrosis.
sections.p: Identify pre‑renal, intrinsic, and post‑renal categories. In East Africa, infectious and toxin‑related causes dominate.

b: AKI: sudden drop in urine, fluid overload, nausea, confusion, flank pain if obstructive.
CKD: gradual fatigue, nocturia, peripheral edema, hypertension, anemia, bone pain (renal osteodystrophy).
Systemic clues: fever (infection), rash (vasculitis), joint pain (lupus), hematuria (glomerulonephritis).
sections.p: Symptoms and signs vary with acuity and chronicity; look for oliguria, edema, hypertension, and systemic clues to a cause.

b: Basic metabolic panel for electrolytes and creatinine.
Urine dipstick and microscopy if microscopy not available – look for casts, cells.
Ultrasound (if available) for size, obstruction, and kidney echogenicity.
sections.p: Prioritise bedside‑available tests; when a test is unavailable, use clinical surrogates.

t.b: Is hyperkalaemia present? – High K⁺ (>5.5 mmol/L) signals need for urgent treatment.
Is there azotemia? – BUN/creatinine ratio >20 suggests pre‑renal cause.
Is there obstruction or chronic scarring? – Dilated pelvis indicates post‑renal; small kidneys suggest chronic disease.

b: Severe hyperkalaemia (>6.0 mmol/L) with ECG changes.
Pulmonary oedema with hypoxia.
Uremic encephalopathy (altered mental status, asterixis).
Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.2).
Rapidly rising creatinine (>0.5 mg/dL per day).
sections.p: Identify life‑threatening derangements that require immediate action.

b: Fluid resuscitation for pre‑renal AKI (crystalloid 20‑30 mL/kg).
Stop nephrotoxins; replace with safer alternatives.
Treat infections: antimalarials, antibiotics for sepsis, antiretrovirals for HIV‑related disease.
Control hypertension with ACE‑inhibitors or ARBs (avoid if hyperkalaemia).
Manage hyperkalaemia: calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, sodium bicarbonate if acidosis.
Dialysis (peritoneal preferred in low‑resource settings) for refractory fluid overload, severe electrolyte disturbance, or uremia.
sections.p: Treat underlying cause first, then provide supportive renal care and prevent further injury.

b: Check eGFR and ACR every 3‑6 months in CKD.
Blood pressure target <130/80 mmHg.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and influenza.
Educate on avoiding NSAIDs, herbal nephrotoxins, and proper hydration.
Screen for anemia and bone disease; treat with iron, erythropoietin, vitamin D as needed.
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring prevents progression and detects complications early.

b: Heart failure – both cause edema and dyspnoea; look for jugular venous pressure, lung crackles, and cardiac auscultation.
Liver cirrhosis – ascites and low albumin; check for stigmata of chronic liver disease and coagulation profile.
Pulmonary embolism – sudden dyspnoea and hematuria may mimic AKI; assess for pleuritic pain and D‑dimer.
sections.p: Distinguish renal disease from other causes of similar presentations.

b: Serum creatinine may be normal in early CKD if muscle mass is low; rely on ACR.
BUN rises with dehydration, not only renal failure; interpret with volume status.
Urine dipstick may miss low‑grade proteinuria; consider quantitative ACR if possible.
sections.p: Be aware of false‑normal or misleading values in low‑resource settings.
